content: 1. Counsel the family on the importance of using Care for Child Development Counseling Cards. Emphasize the need to provide affection and demonstrate love to the child. Encourage caregivers to be attentive to the child’s interests and respond to them appropriately. Praise the child for their efforts in learning new skills. 2. From birth, babies begin to learn. Provide opportunities for the baby to see, hear, move their arms and legs freely, and touch you. Gently soothe, stroke, and hold the baby. Skin-to-skin contact is highly beneficial. 3. Communicate with the baby by looking into their eyes and talking to them. Breastfeeding is an excellent time to engage in this interaction. 4. Encourage play by providing ways for the child to see, hear, feel, and move freely. Slowly move colorful objects for the child to see and reach for. Examples of toys include shaker rattles and large rings on strings. 5. Smile and laugh with the child. Talk to them regularly to foster communication. 6. Offer the child clean and safe household items to handle, bang, and drop. Examples include containers with lids, metal pots, and spoons. 7. Respond to the child’s sounds and interests. Engage in interactive play, such as hiding a favorite toy under a cloth or box and encouraging the child to find it. Play peek-a-boo to stimulate their curiosity. 8. Name objects and people for the child to help them learn. Provide items for stacking, placing into containers, and removing. Examples include nesting and stacking objects, containers, and clothespins. 9. Ask the child simple questions and respond to their attempts to communicate. Help the child count, name, and compare objects. Create simple toys, such as items of different colors and shapes for sorting, or use chalkboards and puzzles. 10. Encourage the child to talk and answer their questions. Teach them stories, songs, and games. Discuss pictures or books with them. Provide books with pictures as sample toys. 11. For newborns up to one week old, emphasize the importance of holding the baby close during feeding, looking at them, and talking or singing to them. 12. If caregivers are unsure how to play or communicate with the child, remind them that children begin to play and communicate from birth. Demonstrate how the child responds to activities. 13. If caregivers feel too burdened or stressed to play and communicate with the child, listen to their concerns and help them identify a trusted person who can share their feelings and assist with the child. Build their confidence by showing them how to perform a simple activity. Refer them to local services if necessary. 14. If caregivers feel they lack time to play and communicate with the child, encourage them to combine play and communication with other caregiving activities. Suggest involving other family members to help with childcare or household chores. 15. If caregivers lack toys for the child, advise them to use clean and safe household objects or make simple toys. Encourage them to play with the child. 16. If the child is not responding or seems slow, encourage the family to engage in additional play and communication activities. Check the child’s ability to see and hear. Refer the child to specialized services if needed. Encourage the family to interact with the child through touch, movement, and language. 17. If the mother or father must leave the child with someone else for a period of time, identify a reliable caregiver who can provide love and attention. Gradually help the child adjust to the new person. Encourage the parents to spend time with the child whenever possible. 18. If the child is being treated harshly, recommend alternative approaches to discipline. Encourage the family to praise the child for good behavior and respect the child’s feelings. Help them understand the reasons behind the child’s sadness or anger. Offer the child choices instead of using negative commands. 19. If the caregiver does not move with the child or controls the child’s movements, advise them to mimic the child’s movements and follow the child’s lead. 20. If the caregiver is unable to comfort the child and the child does not seek comfort from them, guide the caregiver to look into the child’s eyes, speak gently, and hold the child. 21. If the caregiver scolds the child, suggest redirecting the child’s attention from unwanted actions by offering an alternative toy or activity. 22. Praise the caregiver for positive interactions with the child. If challenges arise, provide advice and problem-solving strategies tailored to the caregiver’s situation. 23. For children under six months, encourage caregivers to move the baby’s arms and legs or gently stroke the baby. If the caregiver does not play with the baby, discuss age-appropriate ways to help the baby see, hear, feel, and move. 24. If the caregiver does not talk to the baby, encourage them to look into the baby’s eyes and engage in conversation. 25. For children six months and older, if the caregiver does not play with the child, suggest age-appropriate play or communication activities. If the caregiver does not talk to the child or speaks harshly, provide an activity for them to do together. Help the caregiver interpret the child’s actions and thoughts, and observe the child’s responses and smiles. 26. If the caregiver feels the child is slow to learn, encourage more activities with the child and check their hearing and vision.
